question: Each time I changed my model, I checked its score on the final test data and picked the settings with the highest score. Why can I not trust that evaluation, and which data should I use to choose settings?
expanded_query: each time changed model checked score final test data picked setting highest trust evaluation which should choose

retrieved.title: Keep a Test Set Outside Development
retrieved.passage:
Keep a Test Set Outside Development
[Image description] Original illustration separating training data from an untouched test set
If we keep changing the model after seeing its test score, that score starts guiding development. Keep the final test set untouched until our choices are fixed.
Use validation data to choose settings. The illustrated 80/20 split is only an example; the split should reflect future deployment.

retrieved.title: Cross-Validation Rotates the Held-Out Fold
retrieved.passage:
Cross-Validation Rotates the Held-Out Fold
[Image description] Five rounds each hold out a different fold, then summarize validation scores
Train on four folds; validate on the fifth. Rotate and compare the average and spread.
Use these scores to choose settings. Keep a separate final test set. Use time-aware or group-aware folds when rows are related.

retrieved.title: Reading Model LeaderboardsDeepSWEArtificial Analysis
retrieved.passage:
Reading Model Leaderboards
Each leaderboard tests a different slice of model performance.
DeepSWE
[Image description] DeepSWE version 1.1 leaderboard chart comparing coding-agent scores with average agent steps per task. The screenshot shows 113 tasks and multiple model configurations as of September 3, 2026.
Coding agents: 113 original, long-horizon engineering tasks. Compare task score with cost, output tokens, or agent steps.
Artificial Analysis
[Image description] Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index bar chart comparing current models. Higher bars indicate a higher composite intelligence score.
Broader model comparison: an Intelligence Index built from ten evaluations, with separate views of speed and cost.
Tip
A leaderboard measures its test. The final comparison should use your own tasks and constraints.
